\chapter{Good Afternoon}
\label{ch:hi-good-afternoon}
\hlchaptermodality{33}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can wish someone good afternoon in Hindi and say honestly how rarely \hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर} is actually used.}

Say \hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर} with \hi{दोपहर} in its widened sense, then rank it honestly below \hi{नमस्ते}/\hi{नमस्कार} for everyday afternoons.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[shubh dopahar]{\hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर} (shubh dopahar) — \textquotedblleft{}good afternoon,\textquotedblright{} this arc's rarest greeting}

\label{lesson:HI-C33-shubh-dopahar}



\begin{quote}
You already know \hi{दोपहर}'s meaning widened from \textquotedblleft{}precisely noon\textquotedblright{} to \textquotedblleft{}the afternoon.\textquotedblright{} This greeting rides that widened sense — but it's the least commonly heard of the three you've now met.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर} — \textquotedblleft{}good afternoon,\textquotedblright{} using the widened sense}
\textbf{\hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर}} (\textbf{shubh dopahar}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{good afternoon}\textquotedblright{} — pairs \textbf{\hi{शुभ}} (\textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}) with \textbf{\hi{दोपहर}} used in the \textbf{widened, modern sense} from last lesson: \textquotedblleft{}the afternoon\textquotedblright{} generally, not the narrow etymological \textquotedblleft{}exactly noon.\textquotedblright{} Good news for consistency: this greeting confirms \hi{दोपहर}'s widened meaning is the one people actually reach for here — nobody uses \hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर} to mean \textquotedblleft{}good {[}precise instant of{]} noon.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest: the rarest of the three, not just another formal phrase}
Here's the twist this lesson adds, verified independently rather than assumed from \hi{सुप्रभात} or \hi{शुभ} \hi{संध्या}'s pattern: of this arc's three \hi{शुभ}+timeword greetings, \textbf{\hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर} is described as the rarest} in actual spoken use — even more so than the other two. Sources call it formal/written, note that casual alternatives like \textbf{\hi{आपका} \hi{दोपहर} \hi{शुभ} \hi{हो}} (\textquotedblleft{}may your afternoon be good\textquotedblright{}) exist but are themselves still uncommon, and confirm \textbf{\hi{नमस्ते}}/\textbf{\hi{नमस्कार}} do the real everyday greeting work across the whole afternoon, same as for morning and evening. This isn't just \textquotedblleft{}another formal Sanskrit-style greeting\textquotedblright{} — it's the weakest-attested of the three, a genuine difference in \textbf{degree}, not just the same story repeated a third time.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}shubh dopahar\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}good afternoon,\textquotedblright{} using \hi{दोपहर}'s widened modern sense
  \item the honest ranking — of \hi{सुप्रभात}, \hi{शुभ} \hi{संध्या}, and \hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर}, this one is the rarest in actual spoken use
  \item \hi{नमस्ते}/\hi{नमस्कार} — the real everyday greeting, covering afternoons too
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर} use \hi{दोपहर}'s narrow \textquotedblleft{}noon\textquotedblright{} sense or its widened \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} sense? (\textbf{The widened sense} — \textquotedblleft{}good afternoon,\textquotedblright{} not \textquotedblleft{}good {[}exact{]} noon.\textquotedblright{}) Is \hi{शुभ} \hi{दोपहर} the most, or least, commonly used of this arc's three \hi{शुभ}+timeword greetings? (\textbf{Least} — described as the rarest of the three in actual spoken use.) What covers the real everyday afternoon greeting instead? (\textbf{\hi{नमस्ते}}/\textbf{\hi{नमस्कार}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[au]{\hi{◌ौ} — the same mark, one stroke more}

\label{lesson:HI-S134-vowel-sign-au}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \textbf{\hi{झ}} — what sound does it carry?

Now look at \textbf{\hi{दो}} and find the mark riding on the \textbf{\hi{द}}. The new one is that mark with a second stroke added.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{◌ौ}}
\textbf{\hi{◌ौ}} — \emph{au}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}, so it never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and replaces the \emph{a} built into it.

Where it sits: the \textbf{ā bar on the right, plus a double stroke above}.

Worked through: \textbf{\hi{क}} + \textbf{\hi{◌ौ}} = \textbf{\hi{कौ}} — \emph{kau}.

\subsection*{Script: the pair that differs by one stroke}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{mark} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{above the bar} \\
\midrule
\hi{◌ो} & o & one stroke \\
\hi{◌ौ} & au & two strokes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The only difference is the count}, which makes this the easiest mark in the script to misread and the easiest to fix: when you meet one, stop and count the strokes above the headline.

You already say these, and every one has \textbf{\hi{◌ौ}} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{नौ}} — nine
  \item \textbf{\hi{मौसम}} — weather
  \item \textbf{\hi{चौदह}} — fourteen
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{◌ौ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \textbf{\hi{◌ौ}} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two words and say which mark each one carries
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{दो}  ·  \hi{नौ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{◌ौ} three times, saying \emph{au} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} the one thing that tells the two marks apart
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What vowel does \textbf{\hi{◌ौ}} put on its consonant? (\emph{au}.) How does it differ from \textbf{\hi{◌ो}}? (One more stroke above the bar.) Name a number you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
